It depends on what you mean by freemium. If you mean definitively that you only want a paid model game like WoW or FFXIV with subscriptions, or buy2play like The Secret World or GW2 I don't know what to tell you, as those models are for the huge studios that have the funding to bridge the gap between inception and people actually purchasing the title or subscriptions. There aren't really any unknown gems because the bar to entry is just too high.

If you include free2play games that are "honest," ie only sell cosmetics, pets, mounts and xp boosters you get a lot more to work with. My favorite of the honest ones is probably Firefall, because you really can get anything other than a couple vehicles in the game just from playing. That's just a personal pick that I get the most fun out of, and may not suit your tastes.

If you just want to look around and need some resources I would suggest looking at mmohuts.com and mmobomb.com . I also suggest looking at several publishers to see if they have something that suits you better. There are some games they offer that were created to be triple A titles but just never took off, and several of them are pretty good. Try GamesCampus, Funcom, Webzen, WapPortal and Aeria.

I will make a plug for a small genre of MMOG that I think does get underrepresented: The server-emulated game. My personal favorite being Project1999 - the fan-built version of the original, hardcore Everquest. Definitely not for everyone, but definitely fun for those that are looking for that kind of experience. There's a SWG instance that's in the late development stages too that looks pretty fantastic for those looking for a good sandbox experience.

All of these kinds of games are completely free - they have to be in order to avoid getting sued into a fine red mist. Many have surprisingly active communities of players. The emulated EQ, for example, routinely has at least as many players as they did back in the original games peak, although its only one server, not 30+.

Having your "level" award a fixed number of action points per-day for free, up to some (relatively low) limit.

Making comments, submissions, upvotes, and downvotes all cost different amounts of "action points".

Receiving replies, comments, upvotes and downvotes all award different amounts of action points.

The daily free top-up limit is less than the cost of a single downvote.

Level is increased by receiving upvotes, decreased by receiving downvotes, and also decreases over time with inactivity.

Action points are also subject to a halflife.

If you want to continue with the game analogy, you could also let users spend action points on skills relevant to how they personally use the site (e.g., after x00 comments and reviving y00 upvotes, you can buy an upgrade that makes comments cheaper for you... these upgrades will disable if you level drops too low, but will reenable if/when you work your way back up).
